title: Discernment of the moment (3.52–3.54)
hook: samyama on the single instant and the order of instants brings the knowledge that carries you across
tomorrow: Kaivalya — when purity of mind equals purity of self

segments.voice: Yesterday: omniscience, and your line, refuse the invitation. The gods at the door, declined without clinging and without pride. Did you turn down one comfortable stopping place? Day four hundred seventy-eight.

Two gooseberries sit on a table. Same size, same green, same tiny freckle near the stem. You look at them, then step out of the room. While you're gone, someone swaps them. You come back. Which is which? Nothing on the surface says. The classical commentary uses exactly this puzzle, two identical fruits, to explain today's sutras. And its answer is that someone with the right kind of discernment could tell them apart. Not by color or shape. By time.
screen: `TWO IDENTICAL GOOSEBERRIES.` → `SWAPPED WHILE YOU WERE OUT.` → `WHICH IS WHICH?`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.52: by samyama on the moment and its sequence, knowledge born of discernment. The word for moment is kshana, the instant. The commentary makes it vivid. As the atom is the smallest piece of matter, the instant is the smallest piece of time. And sequence, krama, is just instants following one another without a break. Then the commentary says something startling. An hour, a day, a year: those are put together by the mind. They don't exist out there as things. Only one instant is real at a time. The whole world changes in that single instant, and the past and future are carried in it as what has been and what will be. Then sutra 3.53: from this, you can tell apart two things that look the same, that share kind, marks and place. The two gooseberries. Each one has its own line of instants, its own history, moment after moment. Rest samyama on that, and the swap is plain. Sutra 3.54 names this knowledge. Taraka, the one that carries across, like a ferry over a river. It takes everything as its object, in every way, and it's without sequence. All at once. Not one thing after another, the way the mind usually knows. So book three's tour of powers ends here, not with flying or vanishing, but with seeing the single instant clearly. And there's an ordinary version. Much of what weighs on a person is an hour, a week, a year, piled up in the mind. The instant itself is often light.
screen: `KSHANA: THE SMALLEST PIECE OF TIME.` · `AN HOUR IS PUT TOGETHER BY THE MIND.` · `EACH FRUIT HAS ITS OWN LINE OF INSTANTS.` · `TARAKA: THE ONE THAT CARRIES ACROSS.` · then, large: `THE INSTANT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice rests in the instant. Sit steady and easy. Notice the breath, not this breath as a whole, but this instant of it, the tiny touch of air right now. Then this one. Then this one. When the mind builds something bigger, the rest of the day, the week, notice the building, and come back to this single instant. Light as it is. The bell holds the time.
Discernment of the moment. By samyama on the instant and its sequence, the knowledge that carries you across.
Your line: the instant. Today, when a day feels too heavy, shrink it, not to the hour, not to the minute, but to this one instant, and see what's actually in it. Day four hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras study 3.52–3.54 with the classical commentary's account of the instant, and in meditation practitioners often train attention on the present moment of the breath.

myth: the commentary says hours and days are put together by the mind
only one instant is real at a time; longer spans are mental constructions.
3.53 says two identical things can never be told apart
discernment born of samyama on the instant can tell them apart.
the knowledge of 3.54 works one thing after another
it is without sequence: all at once.

fork.setup: two identical fruits are swapped while you're out. no color, shape or place tells them apart. what lets the discerning one know?
options: each fruit's own line of instants.
fork.reveal: 3.53: by discernment born of samyama on the instant and its sequence, two things alike in kind, mark and place can be told apart.

original.note: Sanskrit kṣaṇa: an instant, a moment; in 3.52, the smallest unit of time.

trapdoor: what you thought: living in the moment is a modern slogan.
what it means: the classical commentary says only the instant is real, and samyama on it brings the knowledge that carries you across.
what a scholar hears: kshana-tat-kramayoh samyamad vivekajam jnanam (3.52); the Bhashya's atom-and-instant analogy and its two identical amalaka fruits; taraka in 3.54.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 3.52 (samyama on the instant and its sequence)
Yoga Sutra 3.53 (telling apart things alike in kind, mark and place)

Yoga Bhashya on 3.52–3.53 (the instant like the atom; time as mental construction; the two amalaka fruits)

notes: The Bhashya's fruit is the amalaka (Indian gooseberry); rendered 'gooseberries'. Confirm the example and its use of the instant-sequence to distinguish them.
Bhashya on 3.52: the instant as the smallest unit like the atom; hours and days as mental constructs (buddhi-nirmana); confirm.
'Book three's tour of powers ends here' simplifies: 3.55 (kaivalya) follows tomorrow.
Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'neither could anyone' from the hook; softened 'most of what weighs on us' to 'much of what weighs on a person'.
